hints: Look at the ring in Fig. 2.1 - each C in the ring already has two ring bonds, so what two small groups must be added to each C to give it four bonds?
Remember how alpha-glucose differs from beta-glucose only at carbon 1 - think about which side the OH is on for the alpha form.
walkthrough:
What a ring glucose needs**
Think of each carbon in the ring as needing four bonds. Two are already used to join the ring. So each ring carbon needs one H and one OH added. That is the basic pattern for all hexose ring sugars.

Getting the alpha position right**
Alpha and beta glucose are identical except at carbon 1. In alpha-glucose the OH on C1 is on the opposite side to the $CH_2OH$ group. So put H and OH the alpha way round on C1, then complete H and OH on the other three carbons to match alpha-glucose.
Final answer: On carbon 1 (right-side C): H above the ring and OH below the ring. On carbons 2, 3 and 4: one H and one OH added in the correct alpha-glucose positions to complete the structure.

hints: Bond C joins two boxes labelled Asp, Pro, Ser - what type of monomer are these, and what bond always joins them in a polypeptide?
Bond D joins the grey ovals in the short carbohydrate chain - what bond always joins sugar monomers together?
walkthrough:
Bond C between amino acids**
Asp to Pro to Ser to Pro to Cys are all amino acids in a polypeptide chain. Amino acids are always linked by condensation between $COOH$ and $NH_2$ to form a peptide bond. So C is a peptide bond.

Bond D between sugars**
The grey ovals form a short carbohydrate chain attached to serine. That is an oligosaccharide. Monosaccharides are always linked by condensation to form a glycosidic bond. So D is a glycosidic bond.
Final answer: C - peptide bond; D - glycosidic bond.

hints: In cell signalling a chemical messenger arrives at the cell surface but cannot enter - what must it do with a membrane protein first?
walkthrough:
Receptors catch the message**
The carbohydrate part of a glycoprotein gives a very specific shape on the outside of the cell. A signalling molecule with a complementary shape can bind to it, like a key fitting a lock. That binding is what starts the signalling response inside the cell.
Final answer: Act as receptors that bind to a specific signalling molecule / ligand.

hints: Secondary structure is held by hydrogen bonds between the $NH$ of one amino acid and the $C=O$ of another nearby - look at Fig. 2.3 to see why proline cannot play its full part in this.
Tertiary structure is held by bonds between R-groups - use Table 2.1 to see which R-group bonds will be rare when cysteine and serine are low.
Now link high hydrophobic proline and leucine to folding - if ionic, disulfide and many hydrogen bonds are missing, what type of interaction is left to hold the 3D shape?
Split your answer into two clear sections to gain all four marks - two linked points about less helix / sheet, and two linked points about less disulfide / hydrogen / ionic bonding.
walkthrough:
Why secondary structure fails with lots of proline**
Alpha-helix and beta-pleated sheet depend on regular hydrogen bonds between the $NH$ group of one peptide bond and the $C=O$ group of another close by in the chain. Fig. 2.3 shows proline loses its N-H hydrogen when it joins a polypeptide, so it cannot donate a hydrogen bond. With a high proportion of proline there is much less hydrogen bonding and much less helix or sheet, leaving more random coiling.

Why tertiary structure is weak with little cysteine and serine**
Tertiary folding is held by bonds between R-groups: disulfide bonds from cysteine $-CH_2SH$, hydrogen bonds from polar groups like serine $-CH_2OH$, and ionic bonds between charged R-groups. Beta-casein is low in cysteine so forms little or no disulfide bonding, and low in serine so forms less R-group hydrogen bonding. Fewer of the amino acids present can form ionic bonds, so overall there is relatively little stable tertiary structure, with folding depending more on hydrophobic interactions of proline and leucine.

Final answer: Less organised secondary structure: high proline means fewer N-H groups available for hydrogen bonding, so less alpha-helix / beta-pleated sheet forms; fewer hydrogen bonds between -NH and -C=O of nearby amino acids. Relatively little tertiary structure: fewer ionic bonds between R-groups; little cysteine so less disulfide bonding; little serine so less hydrogen bonding between R-groups.
